claims.text: The initial RHEA contains mixed BCC and B2 phases with a predominantly continuous B2 matrix.
Working, intermediate-temperature annealing, and aging will invert the microstructure from a continuous B2 matrix to a continuous BCC matrix containing discrete B2 precipitates.
The resulting B2 precipitates will be fine-scale and uniformly distributed.
The inverted BCC-plus-B2 microstructure will remain stable under the proposed high-temperature conditions.
B2 precipitates strengthen the BCC matrix by obstructing dislocation motion.
The B2 precipitation-strengthening mechanism remains effective at about 1000 °C.
A continuous BCC matrix promotes dislocation mobility and thereby preserves room-temperature ductility.
The treatment will increase yield strength at about 1000 °C by approximately 10–20% relative to the as-homogenized alloy.
The treated alloy will retain room-temperature ductility comparable to that of the as-homogenized baseline.
The thermomechanical treatment will cause no significant increase in alloy density.
The as-homogenized baseline has limited high-temperature strength.
The as-homogenized baseline has insufficient ambient-temperature ductility because its B2 matrix is predominantly continuous.
Excessively high annealing temperatures or prolonged aging can coarsen or dissolve the B2 precipitates.
Coarsening or dissolution of B2 precipitates will diminish the proposed strength and ductility benefits.
Changing the elemental composition beyond the intended range may invalidate the treatment benefits.
The magnitude of precipitation strengthening depends on alloy-specific material and microstructural parameters.
Microstructural homogeneity and precipitate stability depend on the precise thermomechanical schedule.
